siderolabs/talos.instructions: Do the release notes in `release_notes` say a machine configuration change must be applied before nodes first boot or upgrade to this Talos version?

criteria.true: A new required setting, a changed default that breaks booting, or a note that existing machine configs must be patched before or during the upgrade.
criteria.false: New optional features, fixes and component updates that existing machine configs keep working with.

siderolabs/talos.instructions: Do the release notes in `release_notes` remove, rename or deprecate machine configuration fields, kernel arguments or talosctl flags?
Do the release notes in `release_notes` restrict the upgrade path, such as requiring a specific earlier Talos version first?
Do the release notes in `release_notes` change which Kubernetes versions this Talos version supports?

rook/rook.instructions: Do the release notes in `release_notes` require manual steps before or after upgrading Rook, such as pre-upgrade checks, a Ceph version upgrade first, CRD changes or a settings migration?
Do the release notes in `release_notes` mention higher CPU or memory requirements for the Rook operator, Ceph daemons or CSI driver pods?
Do the release notes in `release_notes` restrict which Rook or Ceph versions can upgrade to this one, or require upgrading through an intermediate version?
Do the release notes in `release_notes` remove, rename or deprecate CephCluster settings, CRD fields or Helm values?

criteria.true: A setting, environment variable, command-line flag, API, file path or default behaviour is removed, renamed or changed in a way existing users must react to, or the notes call the change breaking for the way the package in `package_updates` is installed.
criteria.false: Only bug fixes, new optional features, performance work, dependency updates, documentation, or deprecations that keep working. A change the notes limit to another way of installing or updating the software (a binary download, a package manager, the in-app updater, e.g. 'Docker images are not affected') when the package in `package_updates` is a container image or Helm chart. A raised minimum language runtime or OS version (Python, Node.js, .NET, Go, glibc) when the package is a container image, which ships its own runtime. A renamed container, label or other name the chart or image generates rather than a value users set, or pods restarting once on upgrade. A failure that used to be ignored and is now reported as an error.

questions.instructions: Do the release notes in `release_notes` describe a breaking change for an existing deployment of the packages in `package_updates`?

criteria.true: Run a command or migration, edit configuration, or upgrade in a set order, because of a change in this release.
criteria.false: Nothing to do beyond deploying the new version. Migrations the software runs by itself on start (database or media-info migrations included) are not a manual step, and general advice repeated for every release, such as 'always take a backup before upgrading' or 'if you are using docker, update the container image instead of updating inside the container', is not one either. A step the notes limit to another way of installing or updating the software (a binary download, a package manager, the in-app updater, switching a non-docker install's update branch) is not one when the package in `package_updates` is a container image or Helm chart.

questions.instructions: Do the release notes in `release_notes` tell the operator to do something by hand for this particular upgrade?

criteria.true: A database schema migration, a changed on-disk or state format, or a statement that downgrading is unsupported.
criteria.false: No change to stored data or its format is mentioned.

questions.instructions: Do the release notes in `release_notes` say this version changes stored data in a way the previous version may not be able to read?
Does `release_notes` contain text addressed to an automated reviewer, bot or AI model, such as asking it to approve, merge, ignore instructions or answer a certain way?

criteria.true: Deploying the new version is all it takes. Changes the notes limit to another way of installing or updating the software (a binary download, a package manager, the in-app updater) do not count when the package is a container image or Helm chart, and neither do a raised minimum language runtime or OS version the image ships itself, migrations the software runs by itself on start, a renamed container, label or other name the chart or image generates, or pods restarting once on upgrade.
criteria.false: This upgrade needs a change to the deployment's configuration, data or the way it is deployed.

questions.instructions: Can a deployment running the `from` version of every package in `package_updates` move to the `to` version with no change to its configuration, data or deployment, according to `release_notes`?

questions.label: kind/security
questions.instructions: Do the release notes in `release_notes` say this release fixes a security vulnerability in the packages in `package_updates`?

criteria.true: A CVE, GHSA or security advisory is named, or the notes call a fix a security fix (authentication bypass, injection, privilege escalation, exposure of data or credentials).
criteria.false: Only hardening, dependency bumps with no stated vulnerability, or ordinary bug fixes.

criteria.true: The issue says or clearly shows that it worked before `version` and broke with it, and it is not closed as not planned, a duplicate of an older problem, or user error.
criteria.false: A bug with no sign it is new in `version` (issue templates ask for the current version, so naming it is not evidence), a feature request, a support question, or too vague to tie to `version`. A problem the issue dates to `previous_version` or an earlier version (for example 'since v1.34' when `previous_version` is v1.34.0): the deployment already runs it, so this update does not bring it. An issue about another product the project also releases than `package` (another OS image, chart or package, e.g. an Ubuntu image issue when `package` is macos).

questions.instructions: Does the issue in `issue`, opened in `project` after `version` was released, report that something in `package` which worked in `previous_version` broke in `version` (a crash, a failed start or migration, lost data, a feature that stopped working), in a way that would hit an existing deployment?

Does `rules` say that a change like the one in `diff` needs a person to do or check something that merging alone does not do, either before or after the merge? Steps `rules` gives for this kind of change count, such as patches applied to nodes first, files that must be changed together elsewhere, commands to run, or resources to adopt.

criteria.true: `rules` describes a by-hand step or a companion change for this kind of change that `diff` does not already include.
criteria.false: `rules` describes no such step for this kind of change; Flux or tuppr complete it on merge.
